The lift device includes a chassis having a rear end and a front end. A rear leveling assembly is coupled to the rear end of the chassis, while a front leveling assembly is coupled to the front end.

The rear leveling assembly includes first and second rear actuators. These actuators are selectively engageable to actively control pitch and roll adjustments at the rear of the chassis. By selectively extending or retracting one or both rear actuators, the rear leveling assembly can adjust the orientation of the chassis relative to a supporting surface.

The front leveling assembly similarly includes first and second front actuators. The front actuators may be selectively fluidly coupled to enable passive pitch and roll control at the front of the chassis. In this coupled state, fluid can move between the front actuators, allowing them to respond to variations in the supporting surface. Alternatively, the front actuators may be fluidly decoupled so that each actuator can be controlled independently, thereby providing active pitch and roll control at the front of the chassis.

A lift device includes a chassis supported by front and rear leveling assemblies. Each leveling assembly includes a pair of actuators positioned on opposite sides of the chassis so that changes in actuator extension can alter both the pitch and the roll of the chassis. The actuators may be hydraulic cylinders, or other suitable linear actuators, connected between the chassis and corresponding ground-engaging or support structures.

During leveling, the rear actuators are actively controlled to raise or lower the rear portions of the chassis. Independent or coordinated operation of the rear actuators allows the system to correct longitudinal inclination, or pitch, as well as lateral inclination, or roll. Sensors may provide information regarding chassis orientation, actuator position, pressure, or ground contact, and a controller may use this information to command the actuators until the chassis reaches a desired attitude.

The front leveling assembly can operate in either a passive mode or an active mode. In the passive mode, the front actuators are fluidly coupled so that fluid displaced from one actuator can flow to the other. This coupling allows the front of the chassis to conform to uneven support surfaces while the rear assembly performs the primary leveling operation. For example, upward movement of one front support may cause a corresponding downward movement of the opposite front support, permitting the front assembly to accommodate terrain variations without imposing excessive torsional loads on the chassis.

In the active mode, the fluid connection between the front actuators is restricted, isolated, or otherwise reconfigured. The front actuators can then be driven individually or together to provide controlled adjustment of the front portion of the chassis. One or more valves may switch the front hydraulic circuit between the passively coupled configuration and the actively controlled configuration. A pump, pressure source, reservoir, and controller may be used to supply and direct fluid to the actuators as required.

The controller may select the operating mode according to the stage of a leveling sequence, the measured orientation of the chassis, support-surface conditions, or operator input. The front assembly may initially remain passive while the rear actuators establish stable support and correct a substantial portion of the chassis inclination. The controller may then place the front assembly in the active mode to complete the leveling process, increase stability, or maintain the selected chassis attitude. Alternatively, the front assembly may remain passive when compliance is desirable.

By combining active rear leveling with a front assembly that can be switched between passive compliance and active control, the lift device can coordinate support at multiple points while adapting to uneven terrain. The arrangement improves leveling flexibility, reduces chassis twisting, and permits precise control of pitch and roll when needed.
outputs.L5:
### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest yet most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it identifies a specific person, place, object, or idea. When we say “the book,” for example, we refer to a particular book that the listener is expected to recognize.

Although it may seem insignificant, “the” brings clarity and precision to communication. It helps distinguish something known or unique from something general. Without it, many sentences would sound incomplete or ambiguous.

This simple word demonstrates how even the smallest elements of language can have an essential role. “The” may contain only three letters, but it connects ideas, guides understanding, and gives structure to everyday speech and writing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract describing a lift device with a chassis, actively controlled rear leveling actuators, and front leveling actuators that switch between passive fluid coupling and active independent control.
counterfactuals.output: A lift device includes a chassis, a lift assembly supported by the chassis, front leveling actuators, rear leveling actuators, and a control system. The rear leveling actuators are independently and actively controllable to adjust a height or orientation of a rear portion of the chassis. The front leveling actuators are selectively operable in a passive mode and an active mode. In the passive mode, fluid chambers of the front leveling actuators are fluidly coupled such that movement of one front leveling actuator causes a corresponding fluid-driven movement of the other front leveling actuator. In the active mode, the fluid coupling is interrupted, and the front leveling actuators are independently controlled to adjust respective front portions of the chassis. The control system selectively transitions the front leveling actuators between the passive and active modes based on an operating condition of the lift device, thereby facilitating chassis leveling, terrain following, stability, or combinations thereof.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an aerial lift chassis leveling system in formal engineering language. Include paired actuators at both ends, rear pitch/roll control, and selectable hydraulic coupling of the front actuators.
counterfactuals.output:
An aerial lift chassis leveling system comprises a mobile chassis having a front end and a rear end, with a pair of laterally spaced, vertically adjustable support actuators disposed at each end. Each actuator is operatively connected between the chassis and a corresponding ground-engaging wheel, axle, or support member to vary the local elevation of the chassis relative to the supporting surface.

The rear actuator pair is independently controllable. Coordinated extension or retraction of both rear actuators produces chassis pitch correction, while differential displacement between the left and right rear actuators produces chassis roll correction. A controller may command the rear actuators in response to pitch and roll signals from one or more inclination sensors, subject to predetermined travel, stability, and operating limits.

The front actuator pair is connected through a selectable hydraulic coupling circuit. In a coupled operating state, hydraulic fluid may transfer between the front actuators, permitting the actuators to articulate in response to terrain variation and thereby promote load sharing while the rear actuators establish chassis attitude. In an uncoupled or locked state, fluid transfer between the front actuators is restricted or blocked so that their respective positions are hydraulically maintained. The coupling state may be selected by an electrically or hydraulically actuated valve under operator or automatic control.

Accordingly, the system uses the independently controlled rear actuators to regulate both chassis pitch and roll, while the selectively coupled front actuators provide either terrain-conforming articulation or fixed positional support, depending on the commanded operating mode. Interlocks, pressure-relief devices, position sensing, and fault monitoring may be incorporated to prevent unintended chassis movement and to maintain the aerial platform within its allowable leveling and stability envelope.

### Exemplary Patent-Style Claims

1. **A lift device comprising:**  
   a chassis having a front portion and a rear portion;  
   a lift assembly supported by the chassis and configured to raise and lower a work platform;  
   first and second front ground-engaging members coupled to the front portion of the chassis by respective first and second hydraulic actuators;  
   at least one rear leveling assembly coupled to the rear portion of the chassis, the rear leveling assembly including at least one controllable actuator;  
   a hydraulic circuit selectively configurable in:  
   (i) a **coupled mode** in which hydraulic fluid is permitted to transfer between the first and second hydraulic actuators such that the first and second front ground-engaging members passively accommodate pitch and roll of the chassis relative to a support surface; and  
   (ii) a **decoupled mode** in which fluid communication between the first and second hydraulic actuators is restricted to permit independent active adjustment of the first and second hydraulic actuators; and  
   a controller configured to actively operate the rear leveling assembly and to selectively place the hydraulic circuit in the coupled mode or the decoupled mode based at least in part on a sensed orientation of the chassis.

2. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein, in the coupled mode, extension of the first hydraulic actuator causes a corresponding retraction of the second hydraulic actuator, and retraction of the first hydraulic actuator causes a corresponding extension of the second hydraulic actuator.

3. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the hydraulic circuit comprises a valve assembly operable between a first state establishing fluid communication between corresponding chambers of the first and second hydraulic actuators and a second state hydraulically isolating the first hydraulic actuator from the second hydraulic actuator.

4. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein, in the decoupled mode, the controller is configured to command each of the first and second hydraulic actuators independently in response to at least one of a chassis pitch signal, a chassis roll signal, an actuator-position signal, a pressure signal, or a ground-contact signal.

5. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the controller is configured, while the hydraulic circuit is in the coupled mode, to adjust the rear leveling assembly to control at least one of chassis pitch or chassis height while the first and second hydraulic actuators passively conform to the support surface.

6. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the controller is configured to transition the hydraulic circuit from the coupled mode to the decoupled mode when at least one of:  
   a measured chassis inclination exceeds a threshold;  
   a platform elevation exceeds a threshold;  
   a difference between positions or pressures of the first and second hydraulic actuators exceeds a threshold;  
   ground contact is lost; or  
   an active-leveling command is received.

7. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the controller is configured to place the hydraulic circuit in the coupled mode during travel of the lift device and in the decoupled mode during leveling or elevation of the work platform.

8. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the rear leveling assembly comprises third and fourth hydraulic actuators coupled to respective rear ground-engaging members and independently controllable by the controller.

9. **The lift device of claim 8**, wherein the controller is configured to coordinate operation of the third and fourth hydraulic actuators with operation of the first and second hydraulic actuators in the decoupled mode to reduce both pitch and roll error of the chassis.

10. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the controller is configured to maintain the rear leveling assembly under closed-loop active control in each of the coupled mode and the decoupled mode.

11. **The lift device of claim 1**, wherein the first and second front ground-engaging members comprise wheels, tracks, outriggers, or support feet.

12. **The lift device of claim 1**, further comprising an inclination sensor configured to generate pitch and roll measurements, wherein the controller determines respective actuator commands using the pitch and roll measurements and one or more target-orientation values.

13. **A method of leveling a lift device**, the method comprising:  
   actively controlling a rear leveling assembly coupled to a rear portion of a chassis;  
   selectively coupling first and second front hydraulic actuators to permit hydraulic fluid transfer therebetween, thereby enabling passive pitch-and-roll accommodation at a front portion of the chassis;  
   detecting a condition for active front leveling;  
   in response to detecting the condition, hydraulically decoupling the first and second front hydraulic actuators; and  
   independently controlling the decoupled first and second front hydraulic actuators, in coordination with the rear leveling assembly, to adjust an orientation of the chassis.

14. **The method of claim 13**, further comprising returning the first and second front hydraulic actuators to a hydraulically coupled condition after the orientation of the chassis is within a target range or after the lift device enters a travel state.

15. **The method of claim 13**, wherein actively controlling the rear leveling assembly continues during both the selective coupling and the hydraulic decoupling of the first and second front hydraulic actuators.

### Exemplary Specification Language

The lift device includes a hybrid leveling system in which a rear leveling assembly is actively controlled while a pair of front hydraulic actuators is selectively operable in passive and active configurations. In a coupled configuration, the front hydraulic actuators are placed in fluid communication such that displacement of one actuator produces or permits a complementary displacement of the other actuator. The front portion of the chassis may thereby articulate passively in response to terrain-induced pitch and roll, while the actively controlled rear leveling assembly regulates chassis orientation, chassis height, or both.

When enhanced leveling authority is desired, a valve assembly isolates the front hydraulic actuators from one another. Once isolated, each front hydraulic actuator may be supplied with or exhausted of hydraulic fluid independently under control of a controller. The controller may then coordinate the front hydraulic actuators with one or more rear actuators to actively correct chassis pitch and roll. Transition between the coupled and decoupled configurations may be based on operating mode, platform elevation, measured inclination, actuator position, hydraulic pressure, ground-contact status, stability limits, or combinations thereof.
